title: What Holds the Pair, and What Lets Go

scenes.visual: THE WORLD, same as chapter 1 (16:9, dark navy background). Chromosomes are rounded rods with a white centromere dot; one homolog BLUE, its partner ORANGE. NO ALLELE LETTERS appear anywhere in this chapter. Cohesin is drawn as small YELLOW rings around the two sister chromatids: rings on the arms are plain yellow; rings at the centromere are yellow with a thin white outline. The synaptonemal complex is a GREY ladder-like zipper between homologs. Shugoshin is a small TEAL shield. Title card 'What Holds the Pair, and What Lets Go' fades in over a faint paired blue and orange chromosome.

scenes.tts: Why does the first division of meiosis part homologs, and not sisters? In mitosis, homologs do not synapse as a pair. Each chromosome lines up on its own, and its sisters part.
scenes.visual: Split screen. Left, labelled 'mitosis': a copied blue chromosome and a copied orange chromosome line up separately at the equator; each splits, one sister to each pole. Right, labelled 'meiosis I': the copied blue and orange chromosomes lie side by side; the whole blue chromosome goes to one pole and the whole orange to the other, sisters still together. A white question mark sits over the right panel.
scenes.narration: Why does the first division of meiosis part homologs, and not sisters? In mitosis, homologs do not synapse as a pair. Each chromosome lines up on its own, and its sisters part.

scenes.tts: In meiosis one, the sisters stay together, and the homologs part. So something must tie each pair, and let go in the right order.
scenes.caption: In meiosis I, the sisters stay together, and the homologs part. So something must tie each pair, and let go in the right order.
scenes.visual: The right panel fills the screen. Faint dotted outlines appear between the sisters of each chromosome and between the two homologs, each labelled with a small '?'.
scenes.narration: In meiosis I, the sisters stay together, and the homologs part. So something must tie each pair, and let go in the right order.

scenes.tts: Start with the sisters. From S phase on, ring-shaped proteins called cohesin tie them together. The rings sit along the arms and around the centromere.
scenes.visual: Zoom onto one copied blue chromosome. Yellow rings snap closed around both sisters along the arms (plain yellow) and at the centromere (yellow with white outline). Label 'cohesin'. A small timeline at the bottom marks 'S phase' as the rings appear.
scenes.narration: Start with the sisters. From S phase on, ring-shaped proteins called cohesin tie them together. The rings sit along the arms and around the centromere.

scenes.tts: In prophase one, the homologs pair along their length. A protein structure called the sin app toe knee mull complex zips them together.
scenes.caption: In prophase I, the homologs pair along their length. A protein structure called the synaptonemal complex zips them together.
scenes.visual: Pull back: the copied blue and orange chromosomes slide together. A grey ladder-like zipper closes between them from one end to the other. Label 'synaptonemal complex'. Label 'prophase I' at top. Four chromatids are now visible side by side; a small tag reads '4 chromatids'.
scenes.narration: In prophase I, the homologs pair along their length. A protein structure called the synaptonemal complex zips them together.

scenes.tts: While they are zipped, crossing over happens. Segments are exchanged between non-sister chromatids, one from each homolog. It starts with a deliberate break in the DNA of one chromatid. The repair copies from the other homolog, and can end in a swap.
scenes.visual: Schematic, labelled 'schematic' in small grey text. One inner blue chromatid shows a single white gap: a break through both DNA strands. No other chromatid is broken. The cut ends shorten slightly; one thin cut end reaches across and threads into the facing inner orange chromatid, and a short bright line copies along it. The joint then resolves: the blue chromatid now ends in orange, the orange chromatid ends in blue. Labels 'one break', 'copies from the homolog', 'non-sister chromatids' and 'crossing over'. The outer sisters stay unchanged.
scenes.narration: While they are zipped, crossing over happens. Segments are exchanged between non-sister chromatids, one from each homolog. It starts with a deliberate break in the DNA of one chromatid. The repair copies from the other homolog, and can end in a swap.

scenes.tts: Later in prophase one, the zipper comes apart. The homologs pull slightly away from each other. But they stay joined where the crossover was. That visible site is a chiasma.
scenes.caption: Later in prophase I, the zipper comes apart. The homologs pull slightly away from each other. But they stay joined where the crossover was. That visible site is a chiasma.
scenes.visual: The grey zipper dissolves. Blue and orange chromosomes ease apart except at the crossover point, where the swapped chromatids form a cross shape. Label 'chiasma'. Yellow cohesin rings remain along all arms and at both centromeres.
scenes.narration: Later in prophase I, the zipper comes apart. The homologs pull slightly away from each other. But they stay joined where the crossover was. That visible site is a chiasma.

scenes.tts: Now look at what ties the pair. The crossover, plus the cohesin on the arms beyond it, holds the two homologs together. In most organisms studied, that is the link the spindle pulls against.
scenes.visual: The arm rings beyond the chiasma glow brighter. A single glowing loop traces from the blue centromere, along the blue sisters, through the chiasma, along the orange sisters, to the orange centromere: one continuous link. The pair moves to the equator; spindle fibres from the top pole attach to blue and from the bottom pole to orange, and the fibres tighten.
scenes.narration: Now look at what ties the pair. The crossover, plus the cohesin on the arms beyond it, holds the two homologs together. In most organisms studied, that is the link the spindle pulls against.

scenes.tts: So what must the cell cut, to let the homologs go at anaphase one?
scenes.caption: So what must the cell cut, to let the homologs go at anaphase I?
scenes.visual: Freeze on the taut pair at the equator. Question card along the bottom: 'What must be cut to let the homologs go?' Two candidate rings blink in turn: an arm ring and a centromere ring.
scenes.narration: So what must the cell cut, to let the homologs go at anaphase I?

scenes.tts: The cohesin on the arms. Once it is cut, the crossover no longer ties the pair. The homologs part, each still made of two sisters.
scenes.visual: Plain yellow arm rings snap open and vanish. The chiasma slips apart. Blue (two sisters, still joined at the centromere by outlined rings) moves to the top pole; orange moves to the bottom. Label 'anaphase I: arm cohesin cut'.
scenes.narration: The cohesin on the arms. Once it is cut, the crossover no longer ties the pair. The homologs part, each still made of two sisters.

scenes.tts: Cohesin at the centromeres has to survive. A protein called shoo go shin protects it until anaphase two. Shoo go shin brings an enzyme, P P two A, to the centromeres. Removing phosphate there is thought to shield cohesin from being cut.
scenes.caption: Cohesin at the centromeres has to survive. A protein called shugoshin protects it until anaphase II. Shugoshin brings an enzyme, PP2A, to the centromeres. Removing phosphate there is thought to shield cohesin from being cut.
scenes.visual: Zoom onto the blue centromere during anaphase I. A teal shield labelled 'shugoshin' sits over the outlined rings, with a small partner shape labelled 'PP2A'. A pair of scissors approaches and bounces off the shield. Small text: 'thought to: removes phosphate'.
scenes.narration: Cohesin at the centromeres has to survive. A protein called shugoshin protects it until anaphase II. Shugoshin brings an enzyme, PP2A, to the centromeres. Removing phosphate there is thought to shield cohesin from being cut.

scenes.tts: So the sisters stay joined into meiosis two. At anaphase two, the centromere cohesin is cut as well, and the sisters part.
scenes.caption: So the sisters stay joined into meiosis II. At anaphase II, the centromere cohesin is cut as well, and the sisters part.
scenes.visual: Label 'meiosis II'. The teal shield fades. The scissors cut the outlined centromere rings. The two blue sisters move to opposite poles. Label 'anaphase II: centromere cohesin cut'.
scenes.narration: So the sisters stay joined into meiosis II. At anaphase II, the centromere cohesin is cut as well, and the sisters part.

scenes.tts: This two-step release is the pattern seen in yeast and mammals, as studied. One cut frees the homologs. A later cut frees the sisters.
scenes.visual: Small inset icons of a yeast cell and a mouse appear beside a two-step timeline: 'anaphase I: arms' then 'anaphase II: centromeres'. Label 'as studied in yeast and mammals'.
scenes.narration: This two-step release is the pattern seen in yeast and mammals, as studied. One cut frees the homologs. A later cut frees the sisters.

scenes.tts: Each link is a point of failure. In mouse eggs, if centromere cohesin is lost too early, sisters reach meiosis two already apart. They can then go to either pole at random. Eggs can end up with too many or too few chromosomes.
scenes.caption: Each link is a point of failure. In mouse eggs, if centromere cohesin is lost too early, sisters reach meiosis II already apart. They can then go to either pole at random. Eggs can end up with too many or too few chromosomes.
scenes.visual: Replay of anaphase I with the teal shield missing: the outlined centromere rings are cut along with the arm rings. In meiosis II the two loose blue sisters drift; both go to the same pole. Two products appear: one with an extra chromatid, one with none, labelled 'too many' and 'too few'.
scenes.narration: Each link is a point of failure. In mouse eggs, if centromere cohesin is lost too early, sisters reach meiosis II already apart. They can then go to either pole at random. Eggs can end up with too many or too few chromosomes.

scenes.tts: As studied in yeast and mammals, two links are cut in two steps. Arm cohesin goes at anaphase one, and the homologs part. Centromere cohesin goes at anaphase two, and the sisters part.
scenes.caption: As studied in yeast and mammals, two links are cut in two steps. Arm cohesin goes at anaphase I, and the homologs part. Centromere cohesin goes at anaphase II, and the sisters part.
scenes.visual: Side-by-side summary panels. Left 'anaphase I': plain yellow arm rings cut, blue and orange homologs moving apart. Right 'anaphase II': outlined centromere rings cut, two sisters moving apart.
scenes.narration: As studied in yeast and mammals, two links are cut in two steps. Arm cohesin goes at anaphase I, and the homologs part. Centromere cohesin goes at anaphase II, and the sisters part.

scenes.visual: End card over the dimmed world, large white text, centred: 'Cutting arm cohesin frees homologs; centromere cohesin holds sisters until anaphase II.' Beneath it, small grey text: 'as studied in yeast and mammals'.
